item.title: How to get into GigaChat's answers and why it links to different sites each time
item.description:
I asked GigaChat questions from sports, finance, B2B, and marketing in two ways: through the GigaChat API and in the chat itself. In total, I collected about 430 answers, roughly evenly split between each method, and checked if each had links to sources. Links were found in 73% of chat answers and 4% of API answers. However, even in the chat, space is limited: there are usually two to three links under an answer, and some of them change when the question is repeated. Read more

item.title: One Brain for Two Computers: Claude Code's Memory on Git and Hooks
item.description:
I finished a piece of a project on my laptop in the evening, sat down at my PC in the morning, and started explaining to the assistant what was done yesterday. The second time this week. By then, it already had memory. A folder with notes on the disk, it writes to it and reads from it itself. The trouble is that the folder was on only one of the two computers. I didn't want to set up cloud storage for this, and even less so pay for note synchronization. In the end, it all came down to a private repository and two hooks of twenty lines of bash. Below: why a cloud folder, Obsidian Sync, and a plugin didn't work, how the script is structured, what broke along the way, and why a separate storage is needed at all if Claude Code has built-in memory. Read more

item.title: [Translation] How AI Changed the Software Market?
item.description:
Hello! My name is Sasha Zhuravlev. I am a venture investor and founder of the Mento vc fund. We invest in startups at the Seed / Series A stages in the USA, and on my Telegram channel, I share how I see the market and make investment decisions. ICONIQ (over $80B under management) releases a report on the performance of software companies every year. And recently, the latest September 2026 report was released. For me, this is one of the most important industry reports, and I've been waiting for it since July (it was released last year in July 2025), constantly checking if it was out yet. Inside, you'll find answers to the following questions: • Why do investors value one software at 9x annual revenue, and another at less than 3x? • How do leaders grow from $1M to $100M ARR in 2-3 years, while others need 5+ years? • How much do companies spend for every dollar earned, and does it pay off? • What has AI already changed in business processes: specific figures? If you invest in software or are building a company in this industry, this report is one of the most useful materials about the market today. My team and I spent a whole week translating it, compiling charts, and adding our explanations. Enjoy reading!

item.title: Asking SIEM in plain language: connecting an LLM assistant to Wazuh
item.description:
Wazuh collects security events well, but to find answers within them, you need to know the query language and hundreds of index fields. An experienced SOC engineer can write a query in a minute, but it's not so easy for colleagues who haven't worked with Wazuh or SIEM systems. The Wazuh dashboard is built on OpenSearch Dashboards, and OpenSearch has a ready-made assistant – OpenSearch Assistant. It's not included in the Wazuh distribution but can be installed with standard plugins of the same version, without modifying Wazuh itself. This is Andrey, head of cloud security at Selectel. In this article, we will install Wazuh, connect our own model, and add a button to the interface that explains any document. Read more

item.title: How I Searched for Sugar-Free Products Using AI
item.description:
Disclaimer. The text of this article was written by a human author (at least, he considers himself one), but it will be about creating texts and code that can (with full justification!) be classified as "neuro-slop." If you are allergic to neuro-slop, it's better not to read further. And now, to the point. At my last two medical check-ups, my blood sugar was found to be elevated. Not that I was particularly surprised, considering I've loved sweets my entire conscious life, and in recent years, I've often used sweets to cope with stress. However, I want to preserve what's left of my health, so to avoid developing full-blown diabetes, I started to drastically reduce my sugar intake. In itself, giving up sugar is not a problem. Fortunately, there are plenty of substitutes available now – choose one you like and that is scientifically approved, and eat to your heart's content. But there's a nuance – hardly anyone eats pure sugar by the spoonful. It usually enters our bodies through other products. And this is where things get interesting. Read more

item.title: We are facing a review crisis: how AI exacerbates the problem of peer review in science
item.description:
AI is actively used not only in commercial but also in scientific programming, for data analysis and visualization. As in other areas, generative AI multiplies both the good and the bad inherent in the established system. It accelerates code creation and calculations, leading to the faster emergence of research results. However, this is followed by a complex chain of verification and dissemination of results, which is not easily scalable with AI. The prospect is unpleasant: we are trying to produce research results much faster than we can verify which of them actually make sense. A single incorrect piece of code can generate a graph, statistics, conclusion, article, and then dozens of new papers citing the first publication. At each subsequent stage, the result will appear increasingly "scientific" (recall the citation index). Ultimately, if we do not change the system of scientific knowledge dissemination, we risk increasingly overlooking incorrect conclusions, and may even descend into pseudoscience. This, in the end, will not accelerate but only slow down progress. Read more

item.title: Where Does AI Live? How I Moved Sound Out of My Head
item.description:
This article is about how a small home experiment with sound led me to a question that, in my opinion, no one is really asking right now: where should an AI assistant live? It all started with one of my projects, also about sound and human movement: a phone in your pocket picks up footsteps, and in your headphones, each step sounds like walking on snow, a forest path, or under stone arches. Spatial sound already works live there. During this work, I found a way to move sound around your head: place it to the left, right, in front, or far away. Like in ASMR, but I choose the location myself, right with my finger on the screen. After playing around, I noticed something that I hadn't encountered as a ready-made tool for the listener. That's what I want to talk about. Read more

item.title: AI Slop: Is It Really That Bad?
item.description:
You open your feed, find an interesting video, and get hooked. Halfway through, you notice something's off. The voice is too even, the picture suspiciously smooth, the plot drags in places. Then it dawns on you that the whole clip was made by a neural network. And you still don't turn it off. Usually, AI slop is just criticized and scrolled past. They say it's cheap mass production, soulless, just for views. But if the video captivated you, did it really become worse because an AI made it? What exactly do we mean when we call content slop? An empty plot, lack of human labor, or the fact that feeds are clogged with similar videos? This calls for a discussion not only about quality but also about how we evaluate content created by neural networks. In this article, we'll explore how in just a couple of years we went from a funny Will Smith eating spaghetti to videos that are almost indistinguishable from real ones. We'll look at why AI content appears in posts, videos, and music, what makes Chinese AI series so engaging, and why businesses love AI slop. Read on

item.title: How I Cleaned AI Markers from Claude Texts: Prompt, Second Pass, and Regex
item.description:
Neural networks write grammatically, which is precisely why their text is recognizable from the first line: em dashes, "it's not X, but Y" constructions, "it's important to understand," "let's break it down." I encountered this with a Telegram bot that converts voice messages into social media scripts and fixed the problem in three layers in one day. In this article, I'll break down how the bot's pipeline works, why prompt instructions weren't enough, why a second neural network pass also didn't save the day, and what ultimately solved the task. All code below is from a working repository; I've slightly simplified variable names. Read more

item.title: Not AI Will Replace People, But People Will Replace AI. And This Is Already Happening
item.description:
If you browse job postings on Headhunter or LinkedIn, sooner or later you'll come across ads looking for someone with five years of experience who can read other people's code without comments, understands multithreading, and is ready to work with a large volume of code written without human involvement. Sometimes, these ads are posted by the same companies that, a year or two ago, boasted in press releases about how they replaced half of their junior developers and almost all manual QA with agents and generation pipelines. You'll pause at the last line of requirements with the same expression you get when reading a medicine's side effects, where the side effect is the illness itself. A year ago, such an ad would have been a joke in the break room, but now similar vacancies are in every other feed, with various titles from the polite 'AI code reviewer' to the honest 'vibe-code cleaner.' Behind them is almost always the same story: a company first paid to remove people from the process, and then paid again, and more expensively, to bring them back, but now as cleaners after a banquet they weren't invited to. There have been several waves of technologies over the past decades that were supposed to eliminate programmers, from visual script editors to no-code builders, and each has rolled back along roughly the same trajectory. The current one is just noticeably faster because so much money was poured into it that losses started being counted earlier than usual. Read more
